title: Only with a teacher
hook: both Mahamudra and Dzogchen are traditionally learned face to face

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dzogchen. Your line: already complete. Today, how both great teachings are passed on.

Two people stop on a woodland path. One whispers: there's an owl. The other looks. Bark, branches, leaves, more bark. Nothing. The first steps behind, lines up a finger beside the other's cheek, and points. Third branch up. Where it forks. That gray lump. And all at once the lump has eyes and a face, and it can't be unseen. A field guide could have described that owl for a year. It took a person, a finger and a moment, side by side. Tibetan teachers say the deepest teachings pass the same way. Today: only with a teacher.
screen: `THERE'S AN OWL.` → `FOLLOW MY FINGER.` → `NOW IT CAN'T BE UNSEEN.`

segments.voice: First, the pointing out. Both Mahamudra and Dzogchen speak of a moment when a teacher points out the nature of the student's own mind. Yesterday's first statement of Garab Dorje was: be introduced directly to your own nature. An introduction needs someone to make it. The mind's nature, Tibetan teachers explain, is so close and so simple that we look straight past it, the way an eye can't see itself. Second, a story the Kagyu tell, which you first met in year three. Naropa was a great scholar, tradition says, honored for his learning. Then he met the wild teacher Tilopa, who for years put him through hardship after hardship and taught him almost nothing in words. In the story, the moment finally came when Tilopa struck him with a sandal, and Naropa saw. What a lifetime of reading had circled around, one face-to-face moment opened. Third, care on both sides. The guru yoga lesson met the advice to examine a teacher. Here it runs both ways: Tibetan texts on teacher and student advise each to examine the other before the relationship begins. A pointing out only means something from a teacher whose own life shows the teaching. Fourth, what's left for everyone else. Books, recordings and lessons like this one can describe these teachings and prepare the ground. Teachers in both lineages say the rest happens in person. Saying so plainly is part of honoring the teaching.
screen: `A TEACHER POINTS OUT THE MIND.` · `NAROPA, TILOPA AND THE SANDAL.` · `EXAMINE EACH OTHER FIRST.` · `SOME THINGS PASS ONLY IN PERSON.` · then, large: `FACE TO FACE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you only learned because someone showed you, side by side: tying a shoe, riding a bike, a prayer, a recipe, how to be kind to someone who's grieving. See their hands, their face, the moment it clicked, and let some thanks go toward them, wherever they are now.
Only with a teacher. In Tibetan tradition, Mahamudra and Dzogchen are learned face to face, when a trusted teacher points out the nature of the student's mind. Today's word.
Your line: face to face. Some things need a finger beside your cheek, not another page. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Tibetan Buddhism, Mahamudra and Dzogchen are traditionally received from a qualified teacher, often after preliminary practices, in a pointing-out instruction given in person; teacher and student are advised to examine each other before the relationship begins.

chat.says: Can't I just learn Dzogchen or Mahamudra from a good book?
options: Books prepare the ground, but both lineages say the pointing out happens in person.
Yes. Read carefully enough, a book does everything a teacher would do for you.
No. Books on these teachings are forbidden, so reading about them is a mistake.
chat.meaning: Both Mahamudra and Dzogchen speak of a teacher pointing out the mind's nature; books can describe and prepare, but the rest happens face to face.

Naropa.meaning: a great scholar who became Tilopa's student

Tilopa.meaning: the wild teacher who taught Naropa

Garab Dorje.meaning: the teacher credited with Dzogchen's three statements

Kagyu.meaning: the Tibetan school of oral instruction

notes: Naropa story: the sandal blow and 'years' of hardship are told as tradition; confirm the details (versions differ).
Advice that teacher and student examine each other, possibly for a long time: attributed generally to Tibetan texts (e.g. Fifty Verses on the Guru); confirm.
The eye-can't-see-itself image is given as how Tibetan teachers explain it; confirm.
The script says the traditions themselves hold that books can only prepare the ground; confirm this is fair to both Kagyu and Nyingma.
The owl-on-a-branch image is the writer's illustration, not a traditional one.
